title: R Madhavan Moved His Entire Family to Dubai So His Son Could Keep Swimming. It Worked.
excerpt: The actor-director on relocating during the pandemic, rating himself ‘6 out of 10’ as a parent, and why he worries that 19-year-old Vedaant’s fame may be growing faster than his maturity.
body:
R Madhavan has played romantic heroes, directed space epics, and navigated three decades of Indian cinema with an uncommon mix of charm and credibility. But the role he seems most invested in right now is one that doesn’t come with a script: being Vedaant Madhavan’s father.

Vedaant, 19, is one of India’s most promising freestyle swimmers. He has won four gold and three silver medals at the 48th Junior National Aquatics Championships, secured five golds at the Malaysian Open, and is training with an intensity that makes most competitive athletes look casual. His daily routine, as he has described it, begins at 4:30 AM. His parents — Madhavan and wife Sarita Birje — are the infrastructure behind that discipline.

The most consequential decision they made wasn’t about coaches or diet plans. It was about geography.

The Dubai Decision

When the Covid-19 pandemic shut down swimming pools across India in 2020, Madhavan and Sarita faced an urgent problem. Vedaant was in the middle of a critical growth spurt during his teenage years — a window that, for competitive swimmers, cannot be wasted. Without pool access, his international career was at genuine risk.

“It was a crucial decision made at the right time,” Madhavan told The Hindu in a 2025 interview. “Vedaant was experiencing a growth spurt, and lacking access to a swimming pool could have jeopardized his international swimming career.”

Sarita flew to Dubai first with Vedaant. Madhavan followed shortly after. The Indian swimming team was also training there at the time, which made the transition smoother. The family has been based in Dubai since — a relocation that began as a pandemic workaround and became a long-term commitment to their son’s ambitions.

‘6 Out of 10’

What’s striking about Madhavan’s public reflections on fatherhood is the absence of the usual Bollywood-dad performance — no chest-thumping pride, no manufactured humility. When asked to rate himself as a parent, he offered a blunt 6 out of 10.

“There are aspects of parenting I wish I could engage in more fully due to my career,” he said. “My wife is far more involved in day-to-day parenting than I am. I tend to focus on offering philosophical guidance and advice to Vedaant.”

It’s a rare admission from a public figure in India, where fatherhood is often framed in absolutes — either the absent patriarch or the self-sacrificing hero. Madhavan seems comfortable occupying the messy middle ground, where a working parent contributes what he can and worries about whether it’s enough.

The Fame Problem

Madhavan’s most interesting concern isn’t about Vedaant’s athletic trajectory. It’s about his growing public profile.

“I’m not concerned with whether he will achieve greater success,” he said. “My primary concern is whether he possesses the wisdom to understand that recognition can be fleeting, and that he must earn further accolades and establish his own identity.”

This is a peculiarly modern anxiety — and one that will resonate with NRI families who have watched their children grow up in the social media age. Vedaant is already a public figure by association with his father, and his own athletic achievements have made him a name in Indian swimming circles. The question Madhavan is raising is whether a 19-year-old can distinguish between earned recognition and inherited celebrity.

The NRI Parent’s Dilemma

The Madhavan family’s Dubai story is, in miniature, the story of thousands of Indian families abroad. Parents who uproot their lives — leaving careers, communities, extended families — so their children can access opportunities that don’t exist at home. The specifics vary (Silicon Valley for tech, London for finance, Dubai for sports infrastructure), but the underlying calculus is the same: the child’s potential justifies the disruption.

What sets Madhavan apart is his willingness to talk about the cost. He doesn’t pretend the move was easy. He doesn’t claim to have all the answers. He rates himself a 6 and means it.

For diaspora families watching from abroad — particularly those who made similar sacrifices and wonder whether it was worth it — Madhavan’s candour is both familiar and reassuring. The swimming medals suggest the Dubai decision was the right one. The parenting? That verdict, as Madhavan seems to know, takes longer to arrive.

Vedaant’s next big competition will be closely watched. But it’s his father’s quieter, more uncertain performance — as a parent navigating fame, distance, and the limits of what he can control — that may be the more compelling story.
